scenes.tts: The first film followed stored food energy through respiration. What makes that process speed up or slow down? Keep the same pea-cell pathway on screen. We will change one condition at a time.
scenes.visual: Hook first. Rebuild the first film's large CREAM pea cell and PURPLE mitochondrion. Reuse its COLOUR MAP exactly: glucose GOLD, oxygen BLUE, carbon dioxide GREY, water CYAN, cell work GREEN, thermal energy ORANGE. The title appears briefly above the pathway, then becomes the question. All cartoons and qualitative gauges are labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The first film followed stored food energy through respiration. What makes that process speed up or slow down? Keep the same pea-cell pathway on screen. We will change one condition at a time.

scenes.tts: The rate of respiration means how fast cells carry out the process. We can track oxygen entering or carbon dioxide leaving over time. Faster motion through the pathway raises both the rate gauge and the output counter.
scenes.visual: BLUE oxygen dots enter and GREY carbon-dioxide blocks leave the carried pathway. A large dial labelled 'respiration rate' and a separate output counter animate together. No numbers appear. The dial and counter carry a permanent 'schematic' tag.
scenes.narration: The rate of respiration means how fast cells carry out the process. We can track oxygen entering or carbon dioxide leaving over time. Faster motion through the pathway raises both the rate gauge and the output counter.

scenes.tts: Start with temperature. In a suitable range, warmer cells usually respire faster. The pathway blocks move more quickly, so oxygen use and carbon dioxide output rise. This does not mean every increase helps.
scenes.visual: A large thermometer rises through a middle band marked 'suitable range'. The same pathway speeds smoothly; BLUE inputs and GREY outputs become more frequent. A schematic rate curve draws upward only across the middle band.
scenes.narration: Start with temperature. In a suitable range, warmer cells usually respire faster. The pathway blocks move more quickly, so oxygen use and carbon dioxide output rise. This does not mean every increase helps.

scenes.tts: Suppose the cells keep getting hotter. Must the rate keep rising forever? Follow the pathway in your mind, then make your prediction.
scenes.visual: The thermometer approaches a red upper zone while the rising schematic curve reaches a covered section. The pathway pauses mid-motion. Question card: 'Hotter forever means faster forever?'
scenes.narration: Suppose the cells keep getting hotter. Must the rate keep rising forever? Follow the pathway in your mind, then make your prediction.

scenes.visual: Deliberate predict pause. Hold the question and covered curve. A ring timer drains while pathway blocks drift gently in place.

scenes.tts: No. Too much heat damages cells, and respiration slows or stops. The curve bends downward in the damaged range. Boiling is an extreme case. It kills the pea cells instead of making them respire faster.
scenes.visual: Reveal the schematic curve bending down in a red band labelled 'cell damage'. Pathway motion stutters and stops. The thermometer then jumps to a boiling icon; the cell fades and gains a clear 'dead cells: no respiration' label.
scenes.narration: No. Too much heat damages cells, and respiration slows or stops. The curve bends downward in the damaged range. Boiling is an extreme case. It kills the pea cells instead of making them respire faster.

scenes.tts: Next, change oxygen. Close the oxygen valve, and fewer blue dots reach the pathway. Respiration that uses oxygen slows. Seal the valve, and the pathway runs on the oxygen left. As that oxygen runs out, respiration with oxygen slows, then stops.
scenes.visual: Reset the same healthy cell. A large valve constricts the stream of BLUE dots. The pathway and schematic rate dial slow together. Close the valve fully: the BLUE dots already inside keep feeding the pathway, then thin out one by one, and the dial sinks gradually to its bottom as the last dot is used.
scenes.narration: Next, change oxygen. Close the oxygen valve, and fewer blue dots reach the pathway. Respiration that uses oxygen slows. Seal the valve, and the pathway runs on the oxygen left. As that oxygen runs out, respiration with oxygen slows, then stops.

scenes.tts: Now change sugar. With too little glucose, the pathway lacks fuel and slows. Add some, and the rate can rise. Keep adding, and another condition becomes limiting. In yeast, a lot of sugar can increase fermentation while respiration with oxygen falls.
scenes.visual: Reset again. A GOLD glucose hopper begins nearly empty, then feeds the pathway and raises the schematic dial. When the hopper overfills, the dial plateaus beside a generic icon labelled 'another factor limits the rate'. A side branch labelled 'fermentation' grows in a yeast inset, without any claim that oxygen is the limiting factor; no molecules are drawn.
scenes.narration: Now change sugar. With too little glucose, the pathway lacks fuel and slows. Add some, and the rate can rise. Keep adding, and another condition becomes limiting. In yeast, a lot of sugar can increase fermentation while respiration with oxygen falls.

scenes.tts: That yeast branch changes how we measure. Fermentation also gives off carbon dioxide. Baker's yeast ferments even when air is present. So most gas in a yeast balloon can come from fermentation. Oxygen use is cleaner for measuring its respiration with oxygen.
scenes.visual: The yeast inset expands. GREY carbon-dioxide blocks leave both the oxygen pathway and the fermentation branch, then inflate one large balloon. The balloon receives two arrows and gains 'rough measure'. A BLUE oxygen counter separates and gains 'cleaner for respiration with oxygen'.
scenes.narration: That yeast branch changes how we measure. Fermentation also gives off carbon dioxide. Baker's yeast ferments even when air is present. So most gas in a yeast balloon can come from fermentation. Oxygen use is cleaner for measuring its respiration with oxygen.

scenes.tts: Each control acts on the same pathway, but the pattern has limits. Temperature helps only within a suitable range. Oxygen matters to respiration that uses oxygen. More sugar helps only until something else holds the rate back.
scenes.visual: Return to the pea cell. The thermometer, oxygen valve, and GOLD hopper orbit the pathway, then settle into three labelled positions. Each label carries its limit: 'suitable range', 'uses oxygen', and 'only to a point'.
scenes.narration: Each control acts on the same pathway, but the pattern has limits. Temperature helps only within a suitable range. Oxygen matters to respiration that uses oxygen. More sugar helps only until something else holds the rate back.

scenes.tts: Respiration releases stored food energy; temperature, oxygen, and sugar change its rate. The picture gives the pattern. Real measurements must show whether the pattern holds and where its limits are.
scenes.visual: The exact rule types above the carried pathway. The three controls make one final gentle adjustment, while the rate dial responds. Then the schematic dial transforms into an empty evidence panel labelled 'measure oxygen or carbon dioxide over time'.
scenes.narration: Respiration releases stored food energy; temperature, oxygen, and sugar change its rate. The picture gives the pattern. Real measurements must show whether the pattern holds and where its limits are.

scenes.tts: The film has not shown the real pea ranges, yeast values, units, or source limits. Those belong in the evidence. Read them next, compare complete data sets, and test the rule rather than trusting the gauge.
scenes.visual: The empty evidence panel fills with blank graph axes, a blank data table, a units badge, and a source-note card. Do not show any data values or trends. The schematic gauge shrinks into a corner with a red label 'model, not evidence'.
scenes.narration: The film has not shown the real pea ranges, yeast values, units, or source limits. Those belong in the evidence. Read them next, compare complete data sets, and test the rule rather than trusting the gauge.

scenes.visual: End card with one line only: 'Respiration releases stored food energy; temperature, oxygen, and sugar change its rate.'
